INTRODUCTION TO TKT
 TKT was first administered in May 2005, since when there have been over 35,000
entries from Centres in approximately 60 countries.
 TKT is suitable for teachers of English in primary, secondary or adult teaching
contexts and is intended for an international audience of non-first language or first
language teachers of English.
 Candidates taking TKT will normally have some experience of teaching English to
speakers of other languages. TKT may also be taken by
 • pre-service teachers
 • teachers who wish to refresh their teaching knowledge
 • teachers who are moving to teaching English after teaching another subject.
 TKT has the following aims:
 • to test candidates’ knowledge of concepts related to language, language use and
the background to and practice of language teaching and learning
 • to provide an easily accessible test about teaching English to speakers of other
languages, which is prepared and delivered to international standards, and could
be used by candidates to access further training, and enhance career
opportunities
 • to encourage teachers in their professional development by providing a step in a
developmental framework of awards for teachers of English.
 Grading of TKT
 Grading takes place very soon after the answer sheets have been received in
Cambridge. Each module is scored out of a total of 80 marks with each correct
answer carrying one mark. Each module is graded separately and certificates are
issued independently for each module.
 The marks required to achieve each band are set according to the following
information:
  statistics on the candidature
  statistics on overall candidate performance
  statistics on individual tasks and questions
  comparison with statistics from previous versions of TKT.
 Results are reported in Bands 1-4, with Band 4 being the highest.
 2

Special consideration
 Special Consideration can be given to candidates affected by adverse circumstances
immediately before or during an examination. Examples of acceptable reasons for
giving Special Consideration include illness and bereavement. All applications for
Special Consideration must be made through the local Centre as soon as possible
after the examination affected.
 Irregular conduct
 Cases of candidates who are suspected of copying, collusion or breaking the
examination regulations in some other way will be considered by the Cambridge
ESOL Malpractice Committee. Results may be withheld because further
investigation is needed or because of infringement of the regulations.
 Notification of results
 Candidates’ certificates are despatched from Cambridge to their local Centres
approximately two weeks after their answer sheets have been received.
 Requests for a check on results may be made through the local Centre, within one
month of the issue of certificates.
 Cambridge ESOL produces the following documents which may be of use in
preparing candidates for TKT:
  TKT Glossary
  TKT Handbook
  Examination report
  Past Paper Pack
  TKT Teaching Resource. See www.CambridgeESOL.org/teach/TKT
  Teacher Portfolio. See www.teacherportfolio.CambridgeESOL.org

Module 3 – Managing the teaching and learning process
 General description and syllabus
 Module format
 Module 3 consists of two parts.
 Timing
 1 hour 20 minutes
 Number of questions
 80
 Task types
 Objective tasks, such as one-to-one matching; 3/4/5-option matching; sequencing; 3-
option multiple choice and odd one out.
 Answer format
 For all parts of this module candidates indicate their answers by shading the correct
lozenges on their answer sheets. Candidates should use a pencil and mark their
answers firmly. Candidates should use an eraser to rub out any answer they wish to
change.
 Marks
 Each question carries 1 mark.

Part 1
 This part of Module 3 tests candidates’ knowledge of the functions of classroom
language, how to adapt teachers’ language according to its audience and purpose,
how to evaluate teachers’ classroom language, how to analyse learners’ language
and categorise learners’ errors.
 Candidates need to demonstrate an understanding of concepts and terminology related to:
 Syllabus area Examples
 the functions commonly used by the teacher
in the classroom
 • identification of a range of functions and typical
exponents
 • appropriacy of use (degrees of simplicity of language,
appropriateness of sequencing, degrees of formality)
 identifying the functions of language used by
learners in the classroom
 Tasks may involve analysis of language
which is not completely accurate.
 • identification of common functions and typical
exponents
 • identification of communicative purpose
 • appropriacy of use
 categorising learners’ mistakes • categorising types of mistakes
 Part 2
 This part of Module 3 tests candidates’ knowledge of the function of strategies
available to a teacher for effectively managing classes (e.g. interaction patterns,
variety of activity and pace, techniques for correcting learners’ oral mistakes) as well
as the roles a teacher can fulfil at different stages of the lesson, in ways appropriate
to learners and to teaching and learning aims.
 Candidates need to demonstrate an understanding of concepts and terminology related to:
 Syllabus area Examples
 the roles of the
teacher
 • common teacher roles and their functions (e.g. building rapport; managing the
teaching space; planning to introduce variety; catering for learning factors;
establishing systems for praise and reward; establishing rules, routines and
procedures)
 grouping learners • common classroom interaction patterns and their uses
 • grouping of learners and reasons for this
 correcting learners • methods of oral and written correction, and their appropriacy of use
 giving feedback • the focus and purpose of feedback
 • ways of giving feedback

Module 3 Version 7
 This report is intended to provide a general view of how candidates performed in
Module 3 of TKT Version 7, and to offer guidance on the preparation of candidates. It
is based on a statistical analysis of candidates’ answers.
 This analysis showed that overall most candidates handled the questions in this
module well. It also showed that the test provided a reliable assessment of
candidates’ abilities and that it discriminated well between weaker and stronger
performance.
 Tasks 1-5 focus on Module 3, Part 1 of the TKT syllabus, tasks 6 -10 on Module 3,
Part 2.
 Task 1, Questions 1 – 8
 This task focused on identifying the purposes of extracts of classroom language
spoken by teachers. Candidates were required to match teachers’ language to
classroom purposes. The task was handled well by stronger candidates but posed a
few problems for weaker ones. These seemed to stem mainly from a lack of
understanding of particular terms i.e. in B eliciting , in C mingling , in G jigsaw task , in I
 concept checkin g . While Part 1 of Module 3 focuses on the role of language in
classroom management, candidates need to understand terms related to
methodology, as much management is often concerned with the organisation and
putting into practice of different aspects of methodology.
 Task 2, Questions 9 – 16
 This task focused on teacher’s use of language, and particularly on its suitability and
effectiveness for managing learning. Candidates needed to match a teacher trainer’s
comments on a teacher’s instructions to examples of the teacher’s instructions. The
task was generally well answered, though weaker candidates struggled with
Questions 10 and 11. Candidates need to remember that language may be
unsuitable not just because it refers to actions that were unsuitable but also because
it may itself be unsuitable or inappropriate. This is the case in these two questions
where the language used is too technical for its audience of elementary learners in
Question 10, and rude in Question 11. There was also evidence suggesting that
weaker candidates may have based their answers on part of an option rather than
ensuring that the whole option matched. This was the case for B and E, both wrongly
matched to Question 15, for example.
 Task 3, Questions 17 – 23
 This task looked at the functions of learner language. The language was set in an
extract from a classroom exchange between a teacher and a learner. Candidates
were asked to answer multiple-choice questions on words or phrases taken from the
extract. This kind of task requires candidates to understand not just the word or
phrase tested but their role and meaning within the extract, so it becomes very
important for the candidate to read the whole extract carefully, especially those words
and sentences around the tested items, as these give the context which shows their
 7

full meaning in the stretch of language they are part of. This kind of task is not
concerned so much with meaning in isolation, but with the meaning that words take
on in discourse. While candidates generally coped well with the task, it was clear
that many found it more difficult than other tasks. Answers suggest that some
candidates may not have read the text and/or the options fully. As with matching
tasks, every word in a multiple-choice task is there for a reason, and needs to be
taken into consideration when answering. It would be useful for candidates preparing
for this task to listen to extracts or watch videos of classroom language so as to see
the role of context in making meaning, and focus on overall and discourse meaning
rather than the meaning of individual words.
 Task 4, Questions 24 – 30
 This task focused on the area of teacher instructions. Candidates were required to
match a teacher’s instructions to the activities being carried out in class. Though
some questions were well answered, this task generally proved more difficult than
preceding ones while discriminating well between stronger and weaker candidates.
The area of instructions is an important one in effective teaching, and when preparing
for this task, it could help candidates to watch videos of teachers giving instructions.
This could lead to discussion of why the instructions were given, whether they were
effective, how they might be improved etc. In the case of this task, Question 25
proved most difficult with many candidates wrongly choosing Option D which
contains a word spot with the question. Similarly for Question 24, which also proved
difficult, many candidates opted (wrongly) for Option C which contained the word
spot read. Candidates are advised to read both the questions and the options
carefully to ensure a match between all parts of them. Detailed reading of Question
24, for example, makes it clear that there is no jigsaw reading taking place.
 Task 5, Questions 31 – 40
 This task focused on the mistakes made in a student’s composition and tested
candidates’ ability to identify what kind of grammatical mistake they were. This was a
four-option matching task in which options could be used more than once as
answers. The task was generally well answered, particularly by stronger candidates.
The reasons for the mistakes made by weaker candidates were not obvious e.g. D
wrongly given as the answer to Question 31, C wrongly given as the answer to
Question 33, or C wrongly given as the answer to Question 39. Candidates are
advised to read the whole text through before answering any one question. This will
give them the general meaning of the text and help them to understand what
students are trying to say at any one point. They are also reminded that there will
only be one mistake amongst the words circled. When preparing for this kind of task,
candidates could usefully work with writing produced by their own students or those
of colleagues. Being able to identify types of error is important to teachers not just for
selecting which types of errors to correct but also for diagnosing students’ difficulties.
 Task 6, Questions 41 – 46
 This task focused on general issues in classroom management. Candidates were
required to match solutions to classroom management problems with the problems
themselves. The problems, such as students working slowing, showing a lack of
 8

interest, ignoring layout and presentation in their writing etc. are problems that
regularly occur in the classroom and that teachers need to deal with on a daily basis.
The task, which was well answered, showed that candidates recognised how the
problems could be solved. Wrong answers showed evidence once again that
candidates had not read or taken on board all the details in the questions or the
options, only matching parts of questions and answers to one another e.g. C, wrongly
given by some candidates as the answer to 42, or B as a (wrong) answer to Question
44. These wrong answers would not directly or fully address the problems identified.
 When preparing for this part of TKT, candidates could be given sets of classroom
management problems and discuss possible solutions to them, or talk about
classroom management problems of their own. There are general strategies for
classroom management, such as catering for all levels in a class, introducing
different kinds of variety to keep students on task, grouping students in different
ways, careful monitoring etc. which can be identified through such activities.
 Task 7, Questions 47 – 56
 This task focused on the kinds of knowledge that teaching calls on and which can be
put to use to help manage learning. The types of knowledge link with the roles that a
teacher has to play in the classroom e.g. as an informant about language (A –
 linguistic), as a user of classroom machinery (E – technological), as someone who
directs learning (B – pedagogical). The task was well handled with only one question
posing some problems for stronger candidates. This was Question 48 where B was
wrongly given as the right answer by a large number of both stronger and weaker
candidates. Some weaker candidates also gave B as the wrong answer to other
questions (49, 50, 55), indicating that they may have been unsure of its meaning.
 Task 8, Questions 57 – 64
 This task focused on the opportunities provided to the teacher by different ways of
interacting with students in the class. Candidates were required to match ways of
interacting with their features, which were in fact advantages. The task was
generally answered well with candidates able to see how different interaction
patterns could be used for different effects. This is useful knowledge for the teacher
to have at their disposal when planning and delivering lessons. Some answers did
indicate however that candidates may not have fully explored these interaction
patterns in their own teaching e.g. some candidates wrongly gave A as the answer to
Question 62 and 63. While interaction pattern A would indeed help the teacher in
both cases, so would B. C thus becomes the answer. When preparing for this part of
Module 3, it would be useful for candidates to watch and analyse videos of
classrooms in action to identify and evaluate the interaction patterns used.
 Task 9, Questions 65 – 70
 This task focused on correction strategies, and in particular asked candidates to
decide on the appropriacy of using particular strategies to correct mistakes in
particular situations. When correcting in class a teacher often has to make snap
judgements about the best correction strategy to employ for particular teaching/
 9

learning situations. The task did not pose any particular problems for stronger
candidates apart from Question 68 for which some of them selected Option B. There
was evidence though that weaker candidates may not have read the rubric. It is
essential that for odd-one-out tasks as with other tasks, candidates read the rubrics.
 Task 10, Questions 71 – 80
 This task focused on feedback. Candidates were asked to match learners’ comments
on different types of feedback with the type of feedback. The task was generally well
handled by all candidates. It was clear from some of the wrong answers, however,
that some weaker candidates had little idea of what peer feedback and echo-
correction were. There was evidence too amongst this group of choosing answers on
the basis of a partial matching e.g. positive things in Question 76 to Option E.
Candidates are strongly advised once again to take on board all the details of both
questions and options before answering.
 RECOMMENDATIONS FOR CANDIDATE PREPARATION
 The recommendations this year are similar to last year’s as answers revealed similar
patterns. Candidates are strongly advised to ensure they have covered all parts and
aspects of the syllabus when preparing for the test.
 They can find the syllabus on pages 25 and 26 of the TKT Handbook or on the TKT
website: http://www.cambridgeesol.org/support/dloads/tkt/tkt_hb.pdf
 Teacher trainers and candidates should note though that no single TKT paper
includes all possible tasks, task focuses or ELT terms. The TKT Handbook lists the
task types, task focuses and terminology that may appear on the paper.
 Module 3 focuses strongly on the classroom, on what happens or develops as the
lesson progresses e.g. instructions, correction, teacher’s or learners’ use of
language. So it is very useful to root preparation for this module strongly in the
classroom. This could take the form of watching videos or listening to recordings of
the classroom, and evaluating them in terms of Module 3 syllabus areas, or
observing others teaching or trying things out in one’s own classroom and reflecting
on the outcomes. Reading websites or books on this part of the syllabus can of
course usefully guide experimentation and reflection.
 The Cambridge ESOL Teacher Portfolio could help candidates with their reflection.
This is available at www.teacherportfolio.cambridgeESOL.org
 Candidates also need to make full use of the TKT Glossary when preparing for
Module 3, by learning the meaning of words, discussing their implications and trying
them out in class when they refer to activities.
 10

DOs and DON’Ts for TKT Module 3
 DO bear in mind the context and who the audience is when answering
 questions on appropriacy of language use.
 DO read the whole text before answering individual questions when the
 task contains a text e.g. a transcript or a student composition.
 DO read and work with any gloss of terms that is supplied.
 DO read each word in the questions and options. Each word is included
 for a reason, and plays a role in pointing towards the right answer.
 DO try to visualise the actual classroom experience described in questions
 when selecting answers.
 DO make sure an option matches all the parts of a question before
 deciding it is the right one. Partial matches will not give the right
 answers.
 DO read rubrics fully, taking note of both the instructions on how to
 answer the task and the context it provides.
 DON’T word-spot answers. Identifying that a word occurs in both a question
 and an option certainly isn’t a basis for matching the question and the
 option. Avoid matching words from the same lexical set too.
 DON’T select answers on the basis of a part match between a question and
 an option. Full matches are required.
 DON’T rely on personal associations between a question and an option. Look
 at the rubric to see what association it requires candidates to look for.
